title: Entering the Pure Land School
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The purpose of studying Buddhism is to become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings. inline.s: The purpose of studying Buddhism is to become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings. For an ordinary being to cultivate and attain Buddhahood there are two great stages: first, to escape the cycle of rebirth; second, to fully realize Buddhahood. The goal of the Buddhist practitioner in this life is to escape the cycle of the six realms of rebirth.

These six realms are: the heavens, the human realm, the asuras, the animals, the hungry ghosts, and the hells. The first three are the three wholesome realms; the latter three are the three unwholesome realms.

Once a sentient being dies, the consciousness, drawn by the power of karma, is reborn in the corresponding realm among the six (birth according to karma). When the force of wholesome karma exceeds that of unwholesome karma, one is reborn in the three wholesome realms; when the force of unwholesome karma exceeds that of wholesome karma, one is reborn in the three unwholesome realms. After the consciousness is reborn, a new phase of life—birth, aging, sickness, and death—begins once more. At the time of death, the consciousness, drawn again by the power of karma, is reborn in the corresponding realm among the six (birth according to karma). Thus birth follows death and death follows birth in endless repetition, like the turning of a wheel; hence it is called “the cycle of rebirth in the six realms.”

The condition for escaping the cycle of the six realms is to extinguish completely all afflictions such as craving and aversion, grasping and rejecting. If a practitioner extinguishes all afflictions, then at the time of death his consciousness gains mastery: he is no longer reborn in the six realms but escapes the cycle, becoming an arhat or a bodhisattva, forever free from birth and death.

How, then, does one extinguish completely all afflictions such as craving and aversion, grasping and rejecting? Taking the Chan (Zen) school as an example, the process is: first, gather the myriad thoughts into one (for instance, by contemplating a huatou, one keeps only this single thought of the huatou); second, return the one to nothing (no thought arises—even the thought of the huatou is gone); then see the nature and awaken to the mind. Afterwards one practices “safeguarding and spontaneous abiding” (baoren) to extinguish the afflictions completely. For an ordinary being to extinguish all afflictions within a single lifetime is exceedingly difficult! Those who succeed are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns. Those who do not succeed are still reborn, at the time of death, in one of the six realms, and continue the cycle. The trouble is that the one reborn suffers the “obscuring veil between lives”—that is, after being born, he knows nothing whatever of his former life or lives. If he is to cultivate so as to end birth and death, everything must begin again from the very start.

Setting aside whether, having become human again in a future life, one would even study Buddhism—merely to obtain a human body again is itself difficult in the extreme! For this reason the Buddha, taking up some earth on his hand, asked Ānanda: “Is the earth in my hand greater, or is the earth of the great ground greater?” Ānanda replied: “The earth of the great ground is greater.” The Buddha said: “Those who obtain a human body are like the earth in my hand; those who lose the human body are like the earth of the great ground.” From this one can see how grave the consequences are if a Buddhist practitioner cannot, in this very life, end birth and death and escape the cycle!

It was precisely in view of this grave situation that Amitābha Buddha, after incalculable, inconceivable, boundless kalpas of arduous cultivation, established the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, opening for sentient beings a golden path upon which all who practice succeed: a sentient being need only, at the moment of death, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in ten continuous, uninterrupted thoughts, and he will evoke the coming of Amitābha to welcome and guide him, be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and thereby end birth and death and escape the cycle. Not only that—once in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one’s lifespan is immeasurable, there is no suffering but only every joy, and the conditions for study and cultivation are supremely excellent; one never retreats again, until one attains Buddhahood.

It must be especially pointed out that the time an ordinary bodhisattva needs to cultivate the path and attain Buddhahood is three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whereas the time Amitābha Buddha needed in his causal stage (as the bhikṣu Dharmākara) to cultivate the path and attain Buddhahood was incalculable, inconceivable, boundless kalpas—many, many, many times greater than the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas! This shows how exceedingly difficult it was to establish the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss—truly beyond conception—and therefore how especially extraordinary it is. Hence Amitābha Buddha is
“the most honored among all lights, the king of all Buddhas”
, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is
“supreme over all the countless Buddha-lands”
Reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss—this is the Pure Land school, abbreviated as Jingzong.
Question: What is the meaning of life?

Answer: The meaning of life lies in awakening—ever greater awakening, until complete awakening (Buddhahood). This process of awakening has three great stages: first, escape the cycle of rebirth; second, realize the unborn (attain the forbearance of the unborn Dharma); third, realize the fruit of Buddhahood. And the meaning of this present life is to escape the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, in this life, whether one is rich or poor, healthy or ailing, whether everything goes smoothly or one meets difficulty upon difficulty—none of this matters. What matters is to end birth and death and escape the cycle, so that, once done, all is done. There are many Dharma gates for ending birth and death and escaping the cycle, but the most direct, the most reliable, and (relative to other Dharma gates) the easiest is to recite the Buddha’s name and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. On this point Master Yinguang and the patriarchs and great masters of all ages have given many teachings and expositions.

Faith, understanding, practice, and realization: faith means to believe in and delight in the Pure Land Dharma gate; understanding means to comprehend the correct path of practice of the Pure Land Dharma gate; practice means to carry out that correct path of practice with one’s whole being; realization means to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death.
Special emphasis is placed here on
“the correct path of practice”

, because in this age of the declining Dharma, false teachers who expound the Dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. If those who recite the Buddha’s name are not extremely vigilant, then at best they go astray (for example, reciting with a scattered mind), heading south while intending to go north, and waste their whole lives in vain; at worst they are lured aboard a pirate ship (for example, the Primal Vow teaching), so that not only can they not be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but, beguiled by heresy, they abet the tiger in its evil, fall into the evil realms at death, and suffer the calamity of sinking for ten thousand kalpas.
As to the correct path of practice, Master Shandao, Master Tanluan, Master Daochuo, and other patriarchs have all given concrete and explicit teachings; see in detail
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
Three Teachings of Master Shandao
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching

Question: Nowadays some groups and websites name themselves with “Pure Land school,” such as the Chinese Pure Land School Association, the Hongyuan Temple of the Pure Land School, and the Chinese Pure Land School
global Pure Land school portal website, and so on. What is going on here?
Answer: This is all the trickery of Master Huijing of the Primal Vow teaching
(for this man’s background see in detail
What Is the Primal Vow Teaching?

The term “Pure Land school” originally referred to the school among the ten schools of Buddhism that exclusively practices Buddha-recitation and seeks rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, with Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty as its founding patriarch,
a great school that has stood alongside the Chan school for over a thousand years

. But their Primal Vow teaching is no more than a tiny faction, and Master Huijing has actually named it “the Pure Land school,” as if they were the entire Pure Land school! This is a deliberate creation of confusion—passing off fish eyes as pearls, passing off the false as the true—in order to deceive people who do not know the truth, especially beginners in Buddhism, so that they mistake them for the Pure Land school and board the pirate ship. This is the very means by which the Primal Vow teaching survives:
deception!
Disciples of the Buddha must open their eyes wide,
and whenever they encounter groups and websites named with “Pure Land school,” they must carefully discern whether they belong to the Primal Vow teaching, so as not to be taken in and deceived

. The method of discernment is simple: if the leading figures are Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and their like, promoting the views and theories of the Primal Vow teaching—for example the Chinese Pure Land School Association, the Hongyuan Temple of the Pure Land School, the Chinese Pure Land School
global Pure Land school portal website, and so on—then these are an outer path that masquerades as Buddhism, the Primal Vow teaching, and not the genuine Pure Land school,
and their true names ought to be: the Chinese Primal Vow Teaching Association, the Hongyuan Temple of the Primal Vow Teaching, the Chinese Primal Vow Teaching
global portal website, and so on. Only then would name and reality match

[The ten schools:] the Kośa school, the Satyasiddhi school, the Chan school, the Tiantai school, the Huayan school, the Mantra school, the Faxiang school, the Pure Land school, the Vinaya school, and the Three Treatise school. [The views and theories of the Primal Vow teaching:] see in detail
The Primal Vow Teaching Is an Outer Path That Masquerades as Buddhism
Question: What is the principle behind rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: The principle behind rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is:
right mindfulness at the moment of death evokes the Buddha’s coming to welcome one.
Master Lianchi said:
“Within, right mindfulness is gathered; without, the Buddha’s welcome is evoked”
(from his Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra).
Master Yinguang, on this principle of rebirth—“right mindfulness at the moment of death evokes the Buddha’s coming to welcome one”—taught:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vows and move the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds, just as the moon appears when the water is clear. But if the mind is impure and insincere, in accord with greed, hatred, and delusion and turned away from the Buddha, it is like turbid, agitated water: though the moon does not withhold its shining, it cannot clearly manifest its reflection in that water.”
(from Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings,
Preface to A Beginner’s Guide to Pure Land Practice).

This means: the minds of sentient beings are like pool upon pool of water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the bright moon in the sky. When, at the moment of death, sentient beings move the Buddha with right mindfulness, the Buddha responds—if the pool water is clear and still, then the bright moon is reflected within it. This is a metaphor for how right mindfulness at the moment of death evokes the coming of Amitābha Buddha to welcome one. If, at the moment of death, the mind is impure and insincere, in accord with greed, hatred, and delusion and turned away from the Buddha, then it is like pool water that is turbid and agitated: although the bright moon in the sky does not withhold its shining, in such pool water the bright moon cannot manifest its reflection clearly. This is a metaphor for how a turbid, agitated, disordered mind at the moment of death cannot evoke the coming of Amitābha Buddha to welcome and guide one.

As to the situation of those who, lacking right mindfulness at the moment of death, become inverted and, drawn by the power of karma, are reborn in the corresponding realm among the six (birth according to karma), Master Lianchi taught:

“Those who are inverted at the moment of death are so because, in their ordinary days, they followed their deluded thoughts, did not cultivate right mindfulness, and had minds that were mostly scattered. At the moment when the warmth of life is about to be relinquished, everything they have done in their lives appears before them; their minds are seized with terror and their movements become frantic. Those who should enter the hells see the mountains of knives and forests of swords as gardens and groves. Those who should fall into the animal realm regard the womb of a horse and the womb of a donkey as grand halls and mansions. Even those who have done good and are due to be born as humans or gods cannot help feeling love and hatred toward their parents. Even the lesser sages at the initial stage of the path cannot yet, with right knowledge, know their going out and coming in. All of this is what is called inversion. Borne by this inversion, within the seven destinies of the three realms they are
reborn according to karma
(from his Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra).

Translation: Those who are inverted at the moment of death are so because, in their ordinary days, they followed their deluded thoughts, did not cultivate right mindfulness, and had minds that were mostly scattered. At the moment when the four great elements are disintegrating, everything they have done in their lives appears before them; their minds are seized with terror and their conduct becomes disordered. Those who should enter the hells take the mountains of knives and forests of swords for beautiful gardens and groves. Those who should fall into the animal realm take the womb of a horse and the womb of a donkey for magnificent halls and palaces. Even those who have done good and are due to be born in the human or heavenly realm, when entering the womb, cannot help loving the mother and hating the father if they are to be male, or loving the father and hating the mother if they are to be female. Even those at the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle and bodhisattvas of the initial aspiration still have the obscuring veil between lives, and cannot, with right knowledge, enter and leave the womb. All of this, every bit of it, is inversion. Because of this inversion at the moment of death, they are reborn according to karma within the seven destinies of the three realms.
[The seven destinies:] the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, humans, the immortals, the gods, and the asuras. “Destiny” means the direction toward which one is bound.
For a more detailed exposition of the principle of rebirth, see
The Principle of Rebirth

Question: I have firmly resolved that I must be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; no matter how hard or how wearying it becomes, I will practice with unflagging diligence. But I must understand clearly what the conditions for rebirth are, so that I will know how to apply myself. Please tell me clearly: what are the conditions for rebirth?

Answer: The condition for rebirth is ten recitations in continuity at the moment of death. That is to say, as long as, at the moment of death, one’s thoughts of Buddha-recitation continue through ten recitations without interruption (without being broken off by deluded thoughts), one attains mutual response with Amitābha Buddha, receives the Buddha’s welcome and guidance, and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore the condition for rebirth can also be expressed as:
ten recitations at the moment of death, and in continuity, rebirth.
For its principle and basis, see in detail
The Conditions for Rebirth
and
Questions and Answers on the Conditions for Rebirth

[Continuity:] the thoughts of Buddha-recitation are linked one after another and are not broken off by deluded thoughts. [Mutual response:] the aspiration of sentient beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha interpenetrate and communicate with one another.
The correct method of Buddha-recitation is single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name, also called mindful recitation that gathers the mind.
This is a way that is settled and never changes.
Master Yinguang taught:
“Reciting the Buddha’s name with a gathered mind,
which is a way that is settled and never changes
(from Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings,
Reply to Layman Liu Guanshan, Letter One). He also taught:
“If the six sense faculties are not gathered in, then even though one recites the Buddha’s name, deluded thoughts still fly about in confusion in the mind, and it is hard to gain any real benefit.”
(from Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings,
Reply to Master Huanxiu). Master Hanshan taught:
“The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; even if you shout till your throat bursts, it is all in vain.”
(from his Song of Wasted Leisure; see in detail
The Song of Wasted Leisure, Annotated
As to why one should recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly, and how to recite single-mindedly, see in detail
Single-minded Recitation of the Buddha’s Name, Not Scattered Recitation
Question: Why is daily nurturing necessary?
Answer: The purpose of daily nurturing is to remove habitual tendencies, dissolve karmic obstructions, deepen faith and vows, and practice in accord with the teachings.
[Karmic obstructions:] the various obstructions in this life created by the various karmic offenses committed in past lives.

What are called habitual tendencies are bad habits: they make you instinctively do what you ought not to do, and fail to do what you ought to do. Every practitioner of Pure Practice knows that to recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is the foremost matter of this life; but how many people actually put single-minded Buddha-recitation first? If one practices earnestly, single-minded Buddha-recitation is not difficult; but how many people actually recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly? And how many people follow the teaching of Master Shandao,
“Restraining the mind and mastering oneself, by day and by night, never ceasing”

? Why do what should be done not get done, and what should be attended to not get attended to, as one drifts with the tide all day and muddles through life? This is habitual tendencies at work. If one muddles along like this, can one be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death? Therefore, in study and practice, removing habitual tendencies is extremely important; one must remove them consciously and deliberately.

Deepening faith and vows is extremely important in Pure Land study and practice; it is the safeguard of practice in accord with the teachings, while practice in accord with the teachings is in turn the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In study and practice, genuine faith and earnest vows and practice in accord with the teachings are like the two wheels of a cart or the pair of wings of a bird—they complement and support each other:
genuine faith and earnest vows are the driving force and the armor
(body-protecting armor)
of practice in accord with the teachings; and practice in accord with the teachings is the actualization and the test of genuine faith and earnest vows.

If one possesses genuine faith and earnest vows, one will certainly practice in accord with the teachings; and the absence of practice in accord with the teachings is precisely the concrete manifestation of faith that is not genuine and vows that are not earnest. However, genuine faith and earnest vows are not attained in a single step (
cù
, to step); they must be gained through long nurturing, by continually deepening faith and vows.
As to the relationship among genuine faith, earnest vows, and vigorous practice, Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, taught:
“Those who do not believe we may set aside
(those who do not believe, put them aside for now and do not speak of them)
. But even among those who believe, one who believes yet has no vow is still
(still)
without belief. One who has vows yet no practice is still
(still)
without vows. One who practices yet not vigorously is still
(still)

without practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vows are not earnest; the reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not genuine. In short, to give rise to genuine faith is difficult. If faith is truly genuine, the vows will of themselves become earnest. If the vows are truly earnest, practice will of itself become vigorous. With genuine faith and earnest vows, joined to bold and vigorous practice, one is certain to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, certain to behold Amitābha, certain to realize the threefold non-retrogression, and certain to attain Buddhahood in his very next life.”
(see in detail
On Buddha-Recitation (Commentary on the Sayings of Master Chewu)
, the chapter “A Single Thought of True Faith”).

[The threefold non-retrogression:] first, non-retrogression of position—the position one has cultivated is not lost; second, non-retrogression of practice—one does not fall back from the practices one cultivates; third, non-retrogression of mindfulness—one does not regress from right mindfulness.
Thus the three provisions of faith, vows, and practice form the core of Pure Land study and practice. The three are an inseparable whole, linked ring upon ring, and their mutual relationship is:
with faith arouse the vows, with the vows guide the practice; with the practice fulfill the vows, with the practice confirm the faith.

These sixteen characters are the fundamental guideline of Pure Land study and practice. That is to say, faith and vows must be carried into vigorous practice before they are genuine faith and earnest vows; and vigorous practice is the actual action by which faith is confirmed and vows fulfilled, and is likewise the yardstick by which to measure how genuine the faith and how earnest the vows are. Those who recite the Buddha’s name must have genuine faith and earnest vows, and practice with vigor.
The Three Character Classic opens with these words:
“People at their birth are by nature good; their natures are alike, but their habits carry them far apart.”

The meaning is that people, at the very beginning, were originally good, and their natures were very much alike. But because of the nurturing influence of their different environments, their natures come to differ greatly. Hence the story of Mencius’s mother moving house three times: by moving several times to choose a good environment in which to educate her child, she at last brought forth a sage of the age. From this we can see how great the power of nurturing is:
one who stays near vermilion turns red; one who stays near ink turns black.

By reading aloud and listening daily to the relevant sutras, treatises, recorded sayings, and teachings—letting ears and eyes be steeped in them, the mind ponder them, and the body put them into practice—this is daily nurturing. Therefore one should “recite constantly and listen constantly, remember constantly and practice constantly, so that body and mind gradually enter the Land of Ultimate Bliss and gradually approach it.” Nurture yourself without ceasing, comprehend the meaning of the scriptures, deepen faith and vows, and practice in accord with the teachings. Please firmly remember:
“Although you strive diligently and endure hardship for a single lifetime, it is but a moment; afterwards you are reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without limit.”
There are many sutras, treatises, and commentaries for daily nurturing, and each person should choose according to his own circumstances. For beginners as an introduction, one may first read:
Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra
Commentary on the Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Reception
and
The Collected Meaning of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life

The power of example is boundless. Real cases of rebirth not only prove the existence of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and prove that Buddha-recitation can lead one to be reborn there, but also set before us a shining example that guides and inspires us to press forward with effort.
